analysis.one_liner: Requires children's websites to get parents' consent before collecting kids' personal information.
analysis.headline: Introduced with bipartisan support and reported favorably by the Senate Commerce Committee in October 1998, the bill never received a Senate vote before the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Federal Trade Commission to write rules requiring commercial websites to follow fair information practices when collecting personal information from children under 16. Websites aimed at children would have to post clear notice of what they collect and get a parent's verified consent before collecting, using, or sharing personal information from kids under 13, and give parents access to the data and a way to stop further collection. The FTC and state attorneys general could enforce the rules, and the FTC could approve industry self-regulation plans as a safe harbor.
analysis.who_benefits: Parents and children under 16 gain control over what personal information websites can collect from kids: notice of collection practices, verifiable parental consent for children under 13, parental access to collected data, and the right to block further use or collection for teens up to 16. The FTC gains enforcement power, and state attorneys general can sue on behalf of their residents.

how_it_helps.text: Websites directed at children would have to post clear, prominent notice of their data collection practices and obtain verifiable parental consent before collecting, using, or sharing personal information from children under 13.

Parents would get reasonable efforts at notice and a chance to prevent or stop collection of data on teens aged 13 to 16, plus access to their own child's collected information and the right to refuse further use or collection.
Operators would have to maintain reasonable procedures to ensure the confidentiality, security, accuracy, and integrity of personal information collected from children.
State attorneys general could sue violators on behalf of residents to stop practices, enforce compliance, and obtain restitution or damages, with the FTC able to intervene.
The FTC would enforce the rules under the Federal Trade Commission Act, treating violations as unfair or deceptive practices, and would report to Congress on implementation after five years.

analysis.who_pays: Commercial website operators, especially sites aimed at children, would bear the cost of building notice, parental-consent, parental-access, and data-security systems within one year of enactment, and would lose the ability to freely collect, use, and sell children's personal information. Online marketers and data brokers that monetized kids' data would lose access to it. Some of these costs could be passed on to consumers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Commercial website operators and online marketers

drawbacks.text: The safe harbor provision allows website operators to comply with industry-written guidelines instead of the FTC's regulations, so long as the FTC approves them, which risks weaker standards being written by the regulated industry itself.

Operators would have to build consent, notice, and security systems within one year of enactment, a compliance cost that falls hardest on small websites, and some of it would likely be passed on to consumers.

Verifiable parental consent is defined loosely as 'any reasonable effort' taking available technology into consideration, which could make the consent requirement difficult to actually verify and enforce.
The tiered age structure (full consent required under 13, weaker notice-and-object rights from 13 to 16) is complicated for parents and operators to navigate, and the protections stop entirely at 16.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is substantial: before this kind of law, websites could collect names, addresses, email addresses, and even Social Security numbers from children with no parental involvement. The bill's costs fall on website operators in the form of compliance systems and lost access to children's data, which is the point of the bill, though small sites would feel the burden most. The design has real soft spots, chiefly the industry-written safe harbor and the loose consent standard, but the overall trade favors families. The main loss here is not the design but the fate: the Senate never voted on it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared the Senate Commerce Committee favorably but was never brought to the Senate floor, and it died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Senator Richard Bryan introduced the bill on July 17, 1998, with Senator John McCain as an original cosponsor, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
The Senate Commerce subcommittee on Communications held hearings on the bill on September 23, 1998.

On October 1, 1998, the Commerce Committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, meaning the committee approved a rewritten version to move to the floor.
No further action followed: the bill never received floor consideration in either chamber, and the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Website operators and online marketers that collected children's personal information were better off in the short run, since the notice, consent, and security requirements of this bill never took effect from it. The bill's bipartisan support and favorable committee report never got a test on the Senate floor.

for.name: Sen. Richard Bryan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its accompanying remarks on July 17, 1998, and moved it through the Commerce Committee.

for.name: Sen. John McCain
for.role: U.S. Senator (R-AZ), original cosponsor and chairman of the Senate Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Signed on as an original cosponsor, and the Commerce Committee he chaired ordered the bill reported favorably with a substitute amendment on October 1, 1998.

for.name: One additional Democratic senator
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, bringing total cosponsors to two (one Republican, one Democrat).

against.name: Senate leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled floor consideration of the bill after the Commerce Committee reported it favorably on October 1, 1998; the record shows no further Senate action before Congress adjourned.

against.name: Website and online advertising industry
against.role: Commercial website operators and online marketers
against.what_they_did: Favored self-regulation over federal legislation governing the collection of children's personal information, and the bill itself carved out an industry-written safe harbor in response.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Democrat with a Republican original cosponsor and cleared the Republican-chaired Commerce Committee favorably; no roll-call votes were ever taken, so there was no party-split vote to measure.

industries.industry: Commercial website operators (especially children's and e-commerce sites)
industries.note: The bill would have required these operators to give notice, obtain verifiable parental consent, provide parental access, and secure children's data, ending the then-common practice of collecting kids' names, addresses, and email addresses without parental involvement. Operators' interest in free data collection ran directly against the privacy interest of families.

Marketers that built profiles from children's personal information would have lost access to that data, since collection and disclosure would require parental consent and parents could block further use.

industries.industry: Computer and internet industry self-regulation bodies
industries.note: The bill's safe harbor provision let operators comply with guidelines written by 'appropriate representatives of the computer industry' if the FTC approved them, giving industry self-regulation a formal, federally recognized role in setting children's privacy standards.
